sections.title: Part 1 · Listening to Problem Solving
sections.instructions: Listen to the conversation and answer the questions.
sections.passage:
AGENT: Customer care, Hollis Home Appliances, this is Brandon.
CUSTOMER: Hi Brandon, Aisha Rahman here. My front-load washer stopped mid-cycle on Sunday with an error code, and there's still water inside. I bought it fourteen months ago.
AGENT: I'm sorry to hear that. Our standard warranty covers twelve months, so it would have expired two months ago. Did you buy a protection plan at the time?
CUSTOMER: I'm honestly not sure. The salesperson mentioned one, but I don't remember signing up.
AGENT: Let me search by your phone number. Yes, I see it. You purchased the two-year protection plan for one hundred twenty-nine dollars. It covers parts and labour, with a fifty-dollar deductible per repair, not per visit, so if a second visit is needed for a part, you won't be charged again.
CUSTOMER: That's a relief. What are my options for a technician?
AGENT: Thursday between eight and noon; Saturday between one and five, with a twenty-five-dollar weekend surcharge; or next Tuesday between one and five.
CUSTOMER: I work Thursday morning and can't leave. Tuesday is too far off with three kids and a washer full of water. Saturday afternoon could work. My son's tournament ends at noon.
AGENT: Then I'll book Saturday. You'll pay the fifty-dollar deductible plus the twenty-five-dollar surcharge, seventy-five in total, once the repair is completed.
CUSTOMER: Fine. Is there anything I should do beforehand?
AGENT: Please don't run the machine again. And someone over eighteen has to be home. If nobody answers the door, there's a forty-dollar missed-appointment fee.
CUSTOMER: Understood.
AGENT: You'll receive a confirmation text on Friday afternoon.

SAM: Have you looked at how we're getting to Ottawa this weekend?
JO: I did. The rental is sixty-five dollars a day, so I figured a hundred thirty for the two days.
SAM: That's just the base rate. There's also twenty cents a kilometre after the first two hundred kilometres each day, and the hotel charges thirty dollars a night for parking.
JO: Ugh, that adds up. It's about four hundred fifty kilometres each way, so nine hundred round trip. Minus four hundred free, that's five hundred kilometres, so a hundred dollars. With the base rate and the parking, we're at two sixty before gas.
SAM: And the train is fifty-eight dollars each way if we book today. Tomorrow it goes up to seventy-nine.
JO: For two people, round trip, that's two thirty-two if we book today. That's cheaper than the car once gas is included.
SAM: The last train back on Sunday leaves at seven-ten, and brunch with my cousin ends around one, so timing isn't a problem.
JO: Then it's the train. The only catch is that the station is a twenty-minute cab ride from the hotel.
SAM: A cab is maybe twenty dollars each way. It's still cheaper.
JO: Okay, I'm booking now.

SPEAKER A: I support making first-year university courses pass-fail. First-year students are adjusting to a new environment, and grades add pressure that discourages them from taking risks. At one university that ran a pilot, students took about twenty percent more courses outside their intended major, and they reported noticeably lower anxiety.
SPEAKER B: I understand the goal, but I'm concerned about motivation. In the same pilot, students studied roughly two hours less per week. When there's no difference between a barely passing paper and an excellent one, many people will do the minimum.
SPEAKER A: That's a legitimate risk, but studying two hours less doesn't mean students learned less; the pilot showed no difference in pass rates. And we could limit pass-fail to the first semester, so students still build good habits afterward.
SPEAKER B: Even so, there's an equity issue. Students from under-resourced high schools often rely on strong early grades to show they belong. Removing grades could hide their progress and make it harder to qualify for scholarships that require a minimum average.
SPEAKER A: That's a fair point, and the answer is probably to let students opt in to receiving letter grades if they want them, rather than keeping the current system.

I am writing to request a review of my mark on Lab 3, which was returned on October 18. I received 71 out of 100. My raw score was 81, and a 10-point late penalty was applied because the portal shows my submission at 2:14 a.m. on October 4, after the midnight deadline.

Thank you for your time.
Marcus Ibarra

Thank you for your email and for attaching the IT notice. I have confirmed with the technology office that the portal was unavailable between 11:20 p.m. and 1:50 a.m. on the night in question. Given this, I have removed the late penalty, and your mark is now 81.

sections.title: Reading Part 3 · Reading for Information
sections.instructions: Read the article and answer the questions.
sections.passage:
In the 1880s, the German psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus memorized lists of nonsense syllables and tested himself at intervals. He found that forgetting was steepest immediately after learning: within an hour, more than half of the material could be lost, and the decline then slowed. His "forgetting curve" remains one of the most replicated findings in psychology.

Later research showed that the curve is not fixed. Each time a memory is retrieved, it tends to become more durable, so reviewing material at increasing intervals, such as a day later, then a week, then a month, can flatten the curve dramatically. This "spacing effect" has been demonstrated with subjects ranging from vocabulary to surgical techniques.

A related finding is the "testing effect": trying to recall information from memory strengthens it more than simply rereading it. In one classroom experiment, students who spent part of their study time quizzing themselves scored about twenty percent higher on a test a month later than those who spent all of it rereading their notes.

Paradoxically, the methods that work best often feel worse. Massed practice, or cramming, produces fluency in the short term, which creates an illusion of mastery, whereas spaced retrieval feels slower and harder. When asked afterward, students often rate rereading as more effective than self-testing, even when their own scores show otherwise. Psychologists call the beneficial struggle a "desirable difficulty."

None of this means cramming is useless. If an exam is tomorrow and the material will never be needed again, massed study may be an efficient choice. But for knowledge intended to last, such as a professional qualification or a new language, spacing offers more durable results for the same total time. Researchers caution, however, that the ideal interval depends on how long a person needs to remember the material, and that no single schedule suits everyone.

questions.explanation: The article explains the spacing effect, the testing effect, and why effective methods feel difficult.

sections.title: Reading Part 4 · Reading for Viewpoints
sections.instructions: Read the two viewpoints and answer the questions.
sections.passage:
The Case for Ending Zoos
By Dr. Imani Osei

Zoos justify their existence with conservation and education, but the record is thin. Only a small fraction of the species kept in zoos are ever released into the wild, and many of the animals on display are not endangered at all. Meanwhile, wide-ranging species suffer. Elephants in zoos live roughly half as long as those in protected habitats, and polar bears and big cats often pace endlessly, a behaviour rarely seen in the wild. The educational case is weaker still: studies suggest that a brief visit changes visitors' attitudes and behaviour very little. Sanctuaries, protected reserves, and immersive technology can teach people about animals without confining them.

Reform, Don't Abolish
By Carlos Ferreira

Accredited zoos do more than display animals. They fund field conservation, run breeding programs, and have helped bring species such as the Arabian oryx and the California condor back from the edge of extinction. Zoos also reach millions of people who will never see wildlife any other way, and personal encounters build support for protecting habitats. A ban would leave thousands of animals with nowhere to go, since most cannot be released. The better path is stricter standards: larger enclosures, better welfare oversight, and an end to keeping species, such as elephants and orcas, that clearly cannot thrive in captivity.

questions.label: Question 1
questions.question: What is the main topic of the two pieces?
options: Whether zoos should continue to exist
questions.explanation: Both authors debate the future of zoos.

questions.label: Question 2
questions.question: How does Dr. Osei view zoos' conservation claims?
options: They are essential to animal research
The record is thin, since few species are released and many displayed animals are not endangered
They have saved most endangered species
questions.explanation: She says few species are released and many are not endangered.

questions.label: Question 3
questions.question: What does Dr. Osei say about elephants in zoos?
options: They live longer than wild elephants
They breed more successfully than wild elephants
They are healthier than other zoo animals
They live about half as long as those in protected habitats
questions.explanation: She reports zoo elephants live roughly half as long.

questions.label: Question 4
questions.question: What does Dr. Osei say about zoos' educational value?
options: A brief visit changes attitudes and behaviour very little
Zoos teach more than school programs
Children learn best by seeing animals
questions.explanation: She says studies suggest a brief visit changes little.

questions.label: Question 5
questions.question: What alternatives does Dr. Osei propose?
options: Sanctuaries, protected reserves, and immersive technology
questions.explanation: She lists sanctuaries, reserves, and immersive technology.

questions.label: Question 6
questions.question: What examples does Ferreira use to support zoos?
options: The Arabian oryx and the California condor
questions.explanation: He cites the oryx and the condor as species brought back from near extinction.

questions.label: Question 7
questions.question: What does Ferreira say would happen if zoos were banned?
options: Thousands of animals would have nowhere to go
questions.explanation: He says most animals cannot be released.

questions.label: Question 8
questions.question: What reforms does Ferreira recommend?
options: Closing all zoos within ten years
Stricter standards and ending the keeping of species that cannot thrive in captivity
questions.explanation: He proposes larger enclosures, better oversight, and ending the keeping of certain species.

questions.label: Question 9
questions.question: On what point do the authors partly agree?
options: Zoos are the best form of education
Some species, such as elephants, do not thrive in captivity
questions.explanation: Osei says wide-ranging species suffer; Ferreira says elephants and orcas cannot thrive in captivity.

questions.label: Question 10
questions.question: Which best describes Ferreira's overall position?
options: Zoos should be run by governments
Zoos should be improved rather than eliminated
Zoos should be replaced with technology
questions.explanation: His title and conclusion call for reform, not abolition.

sections.title: Writing Task 1 · Email
sections.instructions: Write an email based on the task below.

writingTask.title: Writing an Email
writingTask.scenario: You completed a two-day training course six weeks ago. The company promised to email your certificate within two weeks, but you have not received it, and you need it for a job application due this Friday. Write an email to the training coordinator.
instructions: Explain which course you took and what you were promised.
Describe what has happened since and why the matter is urgent.
State clearly what you need and by when.
Keep a polite but firm tone.
writingTask.sampleAnswer: Dear Ms. Chen, I am writing about the certificate for the Project Management Fundamentals course I completed on September 12 and 13. At the end of the course, the instructor told us that certificates would be emailed within two weeks. It has now been six weeks, and I have not received mine, even though I wrote to the general inbox on October 1 and have not had a reply. I need the certificate for a job application that is due this Friday, so the matter is urgent. Could you please confirm whether my certificate has been issued and send a PDF copy by Wednesday, if at all possible? If there is a problem with my registration, please tell me so that I can provide any missing information right away. I would also appreciate the name and phone number of someone I can contact directly if this is not resolved by then. I understand that delays happen, and I appreciate your help in settling this quickly. Thank you for your time. Sincerely, Daniel Okoye, Registration No. 20481

sections.title: Writing Task 2 · Survey Response
sections.instructions: Write a response to the survey questions below.

writingTask.title: Responding to Survey Questions
writingTask.scenario: Your local library has received extra funding. It is asking residents whether the money should be used to keep the building open until 10 p.m. on weekdays, or to expand its digital collection of e-books, audiobooks, and online databases. Complete the survey explaining which option you prefer and why.
instructions: Give at least two reasons for your choice, using specific examples.
Address one possible concern about your choice and respond to it.
writingTask.sampleAnswer: I would prefer to use the funding to expand the digital collection rather than to extend opening hours. First, e-books, audiobooks, and online databases are available to every member around the clock, including people who work evenings and those who cannot travel easily. Extended hours, by contrast, would serve only those who can physically visit after eight. Second, digital collections reach more people per dollar. A single licence can be borrowed by many readers over a year, while evening staffing costs continue every week. Some residents worry that not everyone has reliable internet or a suitable device, and that concern deserves attention. To address it, I suggest using a portion of the funds to lend tablets and portable hotspots, and to offer short workshops that teach older patrons how to borrow digital titles. It would also be wise to review usage after one year so that any unused titles can be replaced with more popular ones. I believe this approach serves the widest range of residents. Thank you for the opportunity to comment.

sections.title: Speaking Task 1 · Giving Advice
sections.instructions: Prepare and speak using the prompt below.

speakingTask.title: Task 1: Giving Advice
speakingTask.scenario: Your younger cousin is about to start university in another country and is worried about managing money. Give your cousin advice on how to budget and avoid financial stress.
tips: Give two or three practical suggestions with reasons.
Use a supportive, confident tone.
Show that you understand the concern.
speakingTask.sampleAnswer: I understand why you are nervous, but a few habits can make money much less stressful. First, I would write down all your fixed costs, like rent and phone, before you arrive, so you know exactly how much is left each month. Then, set a weekly spending limit for food and fun, and track it with a simple app, because small purchases add up quickly. It is also smart to keep a small emergency fund, even just a couple of hundred dollars, for surprises. Finally, look for student discounts and part-time jobs on campus. If you plan early, you will feel much more in control.

sections.title: Speaking Task 2 · Talking about a Personal Experience
sections.instructions: Prepare and speak using the prompt below.

speakingTask.title: Task 2: Talking about a Personal Experience
speakingTask.scenario: Talk about a time when you had to adapt quickly to an unexpected change. Explain what happened, how you responded, and what the outcome was.
tips: Set the scene in one or two sentences.
Describe your actions clearly and in order.
End with the outcome and what it taught you.
speakingTask.sampleAnswer: Last spring, my manager told me on a Monday that our biggest client wanted to move a presentation from Friday to Wednesday. I had only two days to prepare, so I quickly listed what was essential and asked two colleagues to help with the slides. We worked late on Tuesday, and I rehearsed on the train the next morning. The presentation went well, and the client even praised our flexibility. That experience taught me that staying calm and asking for help is the fastest way to handle sudden change.

sections.title: Speaking Task 3 · Describing a Scene
sections.instructions: Prepare and speak using the prompt below.

speakingTask.title: Task 3: Describing a Scene
speakingTask.scenario: Describe a crowded airport terminal when many flights have been delayed by a storm. Include what you can see and hear and how the people around you are behaving.
tips: Describe from a wide view to specific details.
Use sensory and emotional language.
Show contrast between different groups of people.
speakingTask.sampleAnswer: The terminal is packed, and the departure board is glowing red with the word delayed. Travellers are sitting on their suitcases along the walls, while others stand in a long, slow line at the service desk. The air is filled with announcements, crying babies, and the low hum of frustrated conversations. Near the window, a group of children play cards on the floor, and a businessman paces while shouting into his phone. In the middle of the chaos, one traveller is calmly sharing snacks with strangers, and the mood softens for a moment.

sections.title: Speaking Task 4 · Making Predictions
sections.instructions: Prepare and speak using the prompt below.

speakingTask.title: Task 4: Making Predictions
speakingTask.scenario: A woman stands beside a flat tire on a quiet country road at dusk. She is holding her phone up and looking at the screen, and a car is approaching in the distance. Predict what will happen next and explain why.
tips: Use details in the scene to justify predictions.
Use language such as will probably, might, and is likely to.
Give a clear beginning, middle, and end.
speakingTask.sampleAnswer: I think the woman is probably trying to find a phone signal, since she is holding the phone up. The approaching driver will likely notice her and slow down, because it is getting dark and the road is quiet. He might offer to change the tire or to call a tow truck from his own phone. In the end, I believe she will be back on the road within an hour, grateful for the help, and she will probably decide to carry a spare-tire kit and a portable phone charger from now on.

sections.title: Speaking Task 5 · Comparing and Persuading
sections.instructions: Prepare and speak using the prompt below.

speakingTask.title: Task 5: Comparing and Persuading
speakingTask.scenario: Your community group must choose a venue for its annual meeting. Option A is a downtown community hall that seats 150 people, costs $400, and is beside a subway station but has no parking. Option B is a school gymnasium on the edge of town that seats 250 people, costs $250, and has free parking but no public transit. Persuade the group to choose one option.
tips: Choose one option at the start.
Compare seating, cost, and access directly.
Acknowledge one weakness of your choice and respond to it.
speakingTask.sampleAnswer: I recommend the downtown community hall. Although it costs a hundred and fifty dollars more, it is right beside the subway, so members who do not drive, including seniors and students, can attend easily. Last year we had about a hundred people, so 150 seats is more than enough, and the extra gym space would just feel empty. Some will say the lack of parking is a problem, but the subway and nearby public lots can fill that need. Accessibility matters most, so the hall is the better choice.

sections.title: Speaking Task 6 · Dealing with a Difficult Situation
sections.instructions: Prepare and speak using the prompt below.

speakingTask.title: Task 6: Dealing with a Difficult Situation
speakingTask.scenario: You are leading a group project at work, and one teammate keeps missing deadlines, which is putting the whole project at risk. Explain what you would say to your teammate and what you would do to solve the problem.
tips: Describe a calm, constructive approach.
Explain what you would say directly to the teammate.
Mention what you would do if the problem continued.
speakingTask.sampleAnswer: I would start with a private conversation, because I want to understand what is behind the delays. I would say, "I've noticed a few deadlines slipping, and I'd like to help. Is something making the work difficult?" If the problem is workload, I would redistribute tasks or extend a deadline. I would also set shorter check-in dates so any issue appears early. If nothing improved, I would let my manager know, presenting facts rather than blame, and ask for advice on how to protect the project.

sections.title: Speaking Task 7 · Expressing Opinions
sections.instructions: Prepare and speak using the prompt below.

speakingTask.title: Task 7: Expressing Opinions
speakingTask.scenario: Some people believe public transit should be free for everyone in large cities. Do you agree or disagree? Support your opinion with reasons.
tips: State your opinion clearly at the start.
Give two or three reasons supported by examples.
Acknowledge a counterargument and respond to it.
speakingTask.sampleAnswer: I agree that public transit should be free in large cities. First, it would reduce traffic and pollution, because more people would leave their cars at home. Second, it would help low-income residents, who often spend a large share of their income on getting to work. Third, it would speed up boarding, since nobody would need to pay a fare, and that makes buses more efficient. Some argue that it would be too expensive, and that is true. However, the money could come from parking fees or congestion charges, and cities also save on road repairs and health costs. Overall, I think free transit benefits everyone.

sections.title: Speaking Task 8 · Describing an Unusual Situation
sections.instructions: Prepare and speak using the prompt below.

speakingTask.title: Task 8: Describing an Unusual Situation
speakingTask.scenario: You see a photo of an apartment building where every balcony is filled with plants and vegetables, and there is a small farm on the roof. Describe the building to a friend and explain whether you would like to live there.
tips: Start with the most striking features.
Describe what residents might do there.
Give a clear personal opinion with reasons.
speakingTask.sampleAnswer: This building looks like a vertical garden. Green vines hang from every balcony, and I can see tomatoes and herbs growing beside chairs and bicycles. On the roof, there are rows of vegetables and a few beehives, with residents working among them. I would love to live there, because fresh food is just an elevator ride away, and it seems to create a strong community. The only downside might be watering and maintenance, but sharing that work with neighbours could be part of the fun.
